extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners, trademark practitioners, USPTO-enrolled attorneys, and counsel involved in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative final order reviewing an ALJ initial decision in a USPTO disciplinary proceeding against a registered patent attorney; addresses violations of professional conduct rules, jurisdiction, procedural filing requirements for appeals, and sanctioning factors. Useful as a guideline for practitioners on conduct, appeal briefing, and disciplinary sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on disreputable or gross misconduct (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in disreputable or gross misconduct in the course of their practice before courts or the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations include persistent patterns of unauthorized practice, repeated flouting of court orders, and conduct undermining professional integrity. The decision cites multiple findings where pattern-of-conduct supported a §10.23(a) violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners are forbidden from engaging in dishonest, fraudulent, deceitful, or misrepresentative conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include false statements to courts or disciplinary authorities, fabrication of evidence, or other acts that 'stretch and exceed the limits of trustworthiness.' Such conduct is an aggravating factor in sanction determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 10.23(b)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall not engage in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct that wastes judicial or public resources or undermines the orderly administration of justice (e.g., initiating suits without authority, ignoring court orders) falls within this prohibition and supports discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to be adequately prepared (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not handle a legal matter without preparation adequate in the circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequate preparation (e.g., drafting substantive filings without proper authorization or while suspended) can constitute professional misconduct. The ALJ found inadequate preparation when respondent drafted legal arguments while unauthorized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty not to neglect legal matters entrusted to the practitioner (37 C.F.R. § 10.77(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must not neglect a legal matter entrusted to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglect includes abandoning clients (e.g., failing to respond to Office Actions leading to loss of protection) and is a proper basis for discipline and sanctioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to seek lawful objectives for clients through available means (37 C.F.R. § 10.84(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not intentionally fail to seek the lawful objectives of a client through reasonably available means permitted by law and the disciplinary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to pursue a client's lawful objectives (or misrepresenting actions taken) supports findings of inadequate representation and can increase sanction severity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized practice of law prohibition (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's rules, nor assist another in doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance in the decision: practicing in federal courts or state courts without proper admission (including pro hac vice when required), or practicing before the USPTO while suspended, constitutes unauthorized practice. The Order explains that practice before the USPTO in trademark/non-patent matters requires being an 'attorney' as defined in §11.1 and §11.14 and cites §11.5(b)(2) and TMEP §608.01 for activities that count as practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal brief filing requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.55; incorporation of FRAP rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal briefs to the Director must comply with 37 C.F.R. §11.55 and the substantive/form requirements of the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure (e.g., FRAP 28(a)(2),(3),(5)-(10), 32(a)(4)-(6)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required components include appellant's contentions with reasons and citations to authorities and record, concise statement of standard of review for each issue, table of contents, table of authorities, statement of issues, statement of the case/facts, and compliance with page limits and type size. Anti-patterns: wholesale incorporation of the entire record, conclusory paragraph-only challenges without record citations, failing to include tables or issue statements. Consequence: nonconforming briefs may be stricken and provide independent basis to reject appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof for disciplinary violations (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations of the PTO Code or PTO Rules must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Director affirmed the ALJ's findings where the facts met the clear-and-convincing standard; practitioners should expect this burden in OED proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction criteria (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office has disciplinary authority over individuals who are registered and who practice before the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical residency or being outside U.S. borders does not exempt a registered practitioner from USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction; registration and practice before the Office suffice to establish jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature and delegation sufficiency for initiating disciplinary complaints (37 C.F.R. § 11.34(a)(5) considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A complaint signed 'per procurationem' or on behalf of the OED Director can be valid; subdelegation to a subordinate is presumptively permissible absent evidence of contrary congressional intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documentary evidence (e.g., declaration of the Director or Position Description evidencing delegation) can cure signature/formal defects; challenge on signature alone is unlikely to succeed without evidence that delegation was unlawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to subpoena for hearing and admissibility of subpoenaed evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: A party must obtain Tribunal permission to issue subpoenas for hearing testimony or documents and must show the materiality and relevance of the proposed testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: attempting to issue subpoenas without following the §11.38 permission process can result in motions in limine and exclusion of that evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction factors for exclusion or suspension (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(1)-(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: When imposing exclusion or suspension, the ALJ/Director must explain the sanction after considering: (1) whether a duty was violated; (2) whether conduct was intentional/knowing/negligent; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury; and (4) aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order applies these four factors in detail: duty violations (unauthorized practice, neglect), willfulness as intent, actual client injury (dismissals, loss of trademark protection), and specific aggravating/mitigating circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (examples used in sanction analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggravating factors include pattern of misconduct across jurisdictions, multiple disciplinary rule violations, willfulness, and untruthfulness during disciplinary process; mitigating factors include no prior disciplinary history and representation of underserved clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence, number, and severity of aggravating factors can substantially increase sanctions; modest mitigation (e.g., pro bono intent) may lessen but not negate sanctions for serious, repeated misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-discipline obligations and consequences (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58, 11.59 and orders)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplined practitioners must comply with duties under §11.58; the USPTO must notify state disciplinary agencies and courts under §11.59; the Office can dissociate names from Customer Numbers and revoke PKI certificates and bar re-obtaining customer numbers until reinstatement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences ordered included notice to state agencies, dissociation from customer numbers and PKI certificates, prohibition on obtaining Customer Numbers until reinstated, and compliance with duties of disciplined practitioners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of Director's review on appeal (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.55(f), 11.56(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may conduct a de novo review of the factual record on appeal and may affirm, reverse, modify, or remand the ALJ's decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Director afforded de novo authority, failure to comply with briefing rules may provide independent grounds to reject an appeal. Substantive legal arguments must be supported by authorities and record citations for meaningful de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'practice before the Office' for trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)(2) and TMEP guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice before the Office in trademark matters includes consulting or giving advice in contemplation of filing, preparing and prosecuting applications, preparing amendments requiring written argument, conducting opposition/cancellation or concurrent use proceedings, and appeals to the TTAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Activities such as drafting substantive Responses to Office Actions or remaining attorney-of-record while suspended qualify as practice. Claiming corporate-officer status to file is insufficient without supporting evidence and does not excuse unauthorized practice.
